section_title: How does Jesus provide for the crowd?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 10 Then the apostles returned and reported to Jesus all that they had done. Taking them away privately, He withdrew to a town called Bethsaida. 11 But the crowds found out and followed Him. He welcomed them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and He healed those who needed healing. 12 As the day neared its end, the Twelve came to Jesus and said, “Dismiss the crowd so they can go to the surrounding villages and countryside for lodging and provisions. For we are in a desolate place here.”

13 But Jesus told them, “You give them something to eat.” “We have only five loaves of bread and two fish,” they answered, “unless we go and buy food for all these people.” 14 (There were about five thousand men.) He told His disciples, “Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.” 15 They did so, and everyone was seated.

16 Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, Jesus spoke a blessing and broke them. Then He gave them to the disciples to set before the people. 17 They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.

context_lines: The apostles return and report to Jesus. He takes them away toward Bethsaida, but the crowds follow. He welcomes the people, teaches them about God’s kingdom and heals those who need healing.

As evening approaches, the twelve suggest sending the crowd to nearby villages for food and lodging. Jesus tells them to give the people something to eat. They have five loaves and two fish, with about five thousand men present.

Jesus has the people sit in groups. He looks toward heaven, speaks a blessing, breaks the food and gives it to the disciples to serve. Everyone eats and is satisfied, and twelve baskets of pieces remain.
The disciples take part in caring for the crowd through what Jesus supplies. Their lack of food has become the setting for a provision that exceeds what they could have offered on their own.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus’ miraculous provision and care for the crowd, with the disciples serving through what He gives. The Catholic Church also sees the multiplied loaves as pointing ahead to the abundance of the Eucharist, or Lord’s Supper; the bishops’ note draws attention to the similar actions at the later meal. ([Catechism 1335](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_two/section_two/chapter_one/article_3/iii_the_eucharist_in_the_economy_of_salvation.index.html); [USCCB note on Luke 9:16](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/luke/9))
god_plan_lines: Elisha’s feeding of a hundred people supplies an earlier Scriptural parallel. A small quantity of barley bread seems inadequate, yet the Lord’s word promises that the people will eat and have some left over. Luke’s scene shows a far larger crowd receiving abundant food through Jesus. The parallel belongs to the wider story of God providing for His people. ([2 Kings 4:42–44](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_kings/4.htm))

John’s account carries the meaning beyond the meal. After this feeding, Jesus directs people toward food that endures to eternal life and identifies Himself as the bread of life. The provision points toward the One the Father sends to give life to the world. ([John 6:26–35](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/6.htm))
